title: The Event Loop
summary: The **event loop** is the mechanism that lets single-threaded JavaScript run non-blocking async code: it continuously moves work from the **task queue** and **microtask queue** onto the **call stack** whenever the stack is empty, so timers, promises, and I/O callbacks run without freezing the page.

subtopics.title: The call stack
subtopics.explanation: JavaScript executes one thing at a time on a single call stack — a LIFO structure that tracks which function is currently running and who called it. When you call a function it is pushed; when it returns it is popped. While the stack is non-empty, nothing else (no timer, no promise callback) can run, which is why long synchronous work blocks the entire page.

subtopics.title: Web APIs (the host environment)
subtopics.explanation: Async-capable operations like setTimeout, fetch, DOM events, and I/O are not part of the JavaScript language — they are provided by the host (the browser or Node). When you call them, JS hands the work off to the host and immediately continues. The host does the waiting on a separate thread and, when ready, queues a callback for the event loop to pick up later.
subtopics.example: setTimeout(() => console.log('later'), 0); // handed to the browser timer API

subtopics.title: The task (callback / macrotask) queue
subtopics.explanation: When a Web API finishes (a timer fires, a click happens, a network response arrives), its callback is placed on the task queue — also called the macrotask or callback queue. The event loop takes ONE task from this queue per loop tick, but only after the call stack is empty and all microtasks have drained.
subtopics.example: // setTimeout, setInterval, DOM events, and message events all enqueue tasks

subtopics.title: The microtask queue
subtopics.explanation: Promise reactions (.then/.catch/.finally callbacks), queueMicrotask, and async/await continuations go on a separate, higher-priority microtask queue. After each task finishes and before the next render or next task, the event loop drains the ENTIRE microtask queue. This is why promise callbacks always run before setTimeout callbacks.
subtopics.example: Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('microtask')); // runs before any timer

subtopics.title: The loop itself
subtopics.explanation: The algorithm is simple and repeats forever: if the call stack is empty, run all queued microtasks until none remain, then take one task (macrotask) from the task queue and run it, then repeat. Conceptually: drain microtasks, run one macrotask, drain microtasks again, run the next macrotask, and so on.
subtopics.example: // loop: [empty stack?] -> drain microtasks -> run 1 macrotask -> repeat

subtopics.title: Why setTimeout(fn, 0) is deferred
subtopics.explanation: setTimeout(fn, 0) does NOT run fn immediately or even synchronously. It tells the host to enqueue fn as a task after at least 0ms. Because the current synchronous code must finish (emptying the stack) and all microtasks must drain first, fn is delayed until a future loop tick — often noticeably later than promise callbacks scheduled afterward.
subtopics.example: console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('C'), 0); console.log('B'); // A, B, C

subtopics.title: Microtasks before macrotasks
subtopics.explanation: On every loop tick the microtask queue is fully drained before a single macrotask runs. So even if a promise resolves after a setTimeout(0) is scheduled, the promise's .then callback runs first. Newly added microtasks during draining are also processed in the same drain, before yielding to the next task.

subtopics.title: Microtask starvation
subtopics.explanation: Because the loop drains ALL microtasks before doing anything else, a microtask that keeps scheduling more microtasks can starve the event loop: timers never fire, the page never re-renders, and the UI freezes even though no single piece of code blocks. This is a subtle hazard of recursive promise chains or queueMicrotask loops.
subtopics.example: function loop(){ Promise.resolve().then(loop); } loop(); // starves rendering

foundations.overview: JavaScript is single-threaded — there is one call stack and one thing runs at a time. The event loop is what makes that single thread feel concurrent: it coordinates between synchronous code on the stack, asynchronous work handed off to the host's Web APIs, and the queues those APIs feed back into. It guarantees ordering: synchronous code first, then microtasks, then one macrotask, repeating forever.
foundations.formalDefinition: The event loop is a runtime algorithm that repeatedly checks whether the call stack is empty and, if so, fully drains the microtask queue and then dequeues and runs a single task (macrotask) from the task queue, re-rendering and repeating indefinitely.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every async behavior in JS — timers, promises, async/await, fetch, event handlers, animation — is governed by the event loop. Predicting execution order, avoiding UI jank, and understanding why code runs 'later' all require a correct mental model of it. It is one of the most-asked senior frontend interview topics.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a chef (the call stack) who can only do one task at a time. Slow jobs (boiling water = timers, deliveries = fetch) are handed to assistants (Web APIs). Finished jobs go onto two trays: an express tray (microtasks) the chef always clears completely first, and a regular tray (macrotasks) from which the chef takes only one ticket before re-clearing the express tray.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser runs JavaScript, layout, paint, and event dispatch on the same main thread. Between macrotasks the browser can render; microtasks run before that render opportunity. Web APIs (timers, network, DOM) run off-thread and post callbacks back to the queues, which is how the browser stays responsive.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Sequencing UI updates, debouncing input, deferring expensive work with setTimeout, batching state updates, and ensuring promise-based code runs in the right order all depend on event-loop behavior. Frameworks like React, Vue, and Angular schedule work around microtasks and tasks.
foundations.businessImpact: A misunderstood event loop leads to janky, unresponsive UIs and race conditions — directly hurting conversion, retention, and perceived quality. Smooth, correctly ordered async code keeps products fast and reliable.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing the loop lets engineers reason precisely about async ordering, avoid blocking the main thread, fix flaky timing bugs, and choose the right scheduling primitive (microtask vs. macrotask) for the job.
foundations.performanceImpact: Long synchronous tasks block the loop and freeze the UI; microtask starvation can prevent rendering entirely. Breaking work into chunks scheduled across macrotasks keeps the page responsive (the basis of cooperative scheduling and time-slicing).
commonUseCases: Deferring non-critical work with setTimeout so the UI paints first
Using queueMicrotask/Promise.resolve().then to run code after current work but before the next render
Chunking large computations across macrotasks to avoid blocking
Reasoning about the order of promise vs. timer callbacks in async code

commonMisconceptions.myth: setTimeout(fn, 0) runs fn immediately or right after the current line.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It schedules fn as a macrotask; it runs only after the stack empties and ALL microtasks drain — typically after every promise callback queued before it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: JavaScript is multi-threaded because async code runs 'in parallel'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JS execution is single-threaded; concurrency comes from the host running Web APIs off-thread and the event loop interleaving their callbacks one at a time.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Promises and setTimeout share one queue, so order depends on timing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They use separate queues. The microtask queue is fully drained before any macrotask, so promise callbacks beat timers regardless of timing.

interactiveExamples.title: Microtasks beat macrotasks
interactiveExamples.explanation: Even though setTimeout is scheduled first, the promise's microtask drains before the timer's macrotask runs.

codeLab.instructions: Without changing the scheduling, add the missing logs so the program prints exactly: 1, 4, 3, 2. Use a microtask for 3 and a macrotask for 2 so they slot into the right ticks.
hints: Synchronous logs (1 and 4) always print first, in order.

debuggingLab.title: Microtask starvation freezes the page
debuggingLab.symptom: The setTimeout callback never logs and the UI stops responding, even though no single line blocks for long.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The event loop drains the ENTIRE microtask queue before running any macrotask. Because spin schedules a new microtask every time it runs, the microtask queue never empties, so the loop never reaches the setTimeout task. Rendering and timers are starved.
commonMistakes: Assuming the loop alternates one microtask then one macrotask.
Believing an infinite promise chain yields to timers or rendering between iterations.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Let the timer fire by scheduling the recursion as a macrotask (or bounding it) so the microtask queue can drain.

theory.question: What is the event loop and how does it make single-threaded JavaScript non-blocking?
theory.directAnswer: The event loop is a runtime algorithm that, whenever the call stack is empty, drains all microtasks and then runs one macrotask, repeating forever. Async operations are handed to host Web APIs that run off-thread and post their callbacks back to queues, so the single JS thread never has to wait — it just keeps picking up completed work.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A coordinator between the call stack, the host Web APIs, the microtask queue, and the task (macrotask) queue.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript has one thread, so it needs a way to handle slow operations (timers, network, I/O) without blocking; the loop interleaves their callbacks with normal code.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Synchronous code runs on the stack; async calls offload to Web APIs; when the stack empties, the loop drains every microtask, then runs a single macrotask, then repeats — with a render opportunity between macrotasks.

theory.whyImportant: It governs the execution order of all async code and is the key to avoiding UI jank and timing bugs; it's a hallmark senior-level interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: When you click a button, the handler runs as a macrotask; any promise it awaits resolves as a microtask before the browser paints the resulting DOM change.

nestedTopics.title: Call stack
nestedTopics.explanation: The single LIFO stack where synchronous code runs one frame at a time.

nestedTopics.title: Web APIs
nestedTopics.explanation: Host-provided async capabilities that run off the main thread and queue callbacks.

nestedTopics.title: Two queues
nestedTopics.explanation: Microtasks drain fully each tick; macrotasks run one per tick.

followUps.question: Where do async/await continuations run?
followUps.answer: The code after an await is scheduled as a microtask when the awaited promise settles, so it runs before the next macrotask.

followUps.question: When can the browser paint?
followUps.answer: Between macrotasks, after the microtask queue is drained — so long tasks or microtask floods block rendering.

theory.question: Why does Promise.resolve().then(...) run before setTimeout(..., 0) even when the timeout is scheduled first?
theory.directAnswer: Because promises use the microtask queue and setTimeout uses the macrotask (task) queue. On each loop tick the event loop fully drains the microtask queue before running any macrotask, so the promise callback always runs first regardless of scheduling order.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A priority difference between two distinct queues the event loop services.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Microtasks exist so promise reactions can settle deterministically and quickly after the current operation, before yielding to lower-priority tasks or rendering.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: After the stack empties, the loop runs ALL microtasks (including ones added during draining), then takes exactly one macrotask, then drains microtasks again.

theory.whyImportant: Predicting this ordering is a classic interview filter and prevents real race conditions in async code.
theory.realWorldExample: Batching DOM reads/writes after a state change relies on microtasks running before the next paint.

nestedTopics.title: Microtask queue
nestedTopics.explanation: Holds promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks; drained fully each tick.

nestedTopics.title: Macrotask queue
nestedTopics.explanation: Holds timer, event, and message callbacks; one runs per tick.

followUps.question: What if a microtask schedules another microtask?
followUps.answer: It is processed within the same drain, before any macrotask — which is how microtask starvation happens.

scenario.question: A page becomes unresponsive: timers stop firing and the UI never updates, but the CPU is busy and there's no error. How do you diagnose it?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd suspect either a long synchronous task blocking the stack or microtask starvation — a promise/queueMicrotask chain that keeps re-scheduling itself so the microtask queue never empties and the loop never reaches timers or rendering. I'd profile the main thread in DevTools to see a single long task or a flood of microtasks, then break the work into macrotasks (setTimeout/requestIdleCallback) so the loop can breathe.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A main-thread blockage caused by never yielding control back to the event loop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The loop only advances when the stack empties and microtasks drain; recursive microtasks or long synchronous loops prevent that.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Chunking work across macrotasks lets the loop interleave rendering, timers, and input handling between chunks.

scenario.whyImportant: It mirrors real production freezes and tests whether the candidate truly understands queue priority and yielding.

nestedTopics.title: Long tasks
nestedTopics.explanation: Synchronous work over ~50ms blocks input and paint.

nestedTopics.title: Yielding
nestedTopics.explanation: Scheduling continuation as a macrotask returns control to the loop.

followUps.question: Which tool confirms the cause?
followUps.answer: The Performance panel's main-thread flame chart shows one giant task (sync block) or continuous microtask activity (starvation).

coding.question: Predict the exact console output of this program and explain the ordering.
coding.thoughtProcess: I separate synchronous logs (run immediately, in order) from microtasks (promise .then, async continuations) and macrotasks (setTimeout). Synchronous first, then the full microtask drain, then macrotasks one at a time.
coding.lineByLine: '1' and '5' are synchronous and print first in source order. setTimeout queues '2' as a macrotask. The first .then queues '3' as a microtask; when it runs it returns a value, queuing the second .then ('4') which is also processed in the same microtask drain. Only after the microtask queue is empty does the loop run the '2' macrotask.

alternativeApproaches.title: Mix in await
alternativeApproaches.explanation: An async function's code after await behaves like a .then microtask, slotting before macrotasks.
alternativeApproaches.code: async function f(){ console.log('a'); await 0; console.log('b'); } f();

followUps.question: If a .then logs and also calls setTimeout, when does that timer run?
followUps.answer: Its callback is queued as a macrotask and runs after the current microtask drain completes, on a later tick.

systemDesign.question: Design a client-side scheduler that runs a large batch of CPU work (e.g., processing 100k items) without freezing the UI. How do you use the event loop?
systemDesign.directAnswer: I'd cooperatively yield to the event loop by chunking the work: process a slice of items, then schedule the next slice as a macrotask (setTimeout, MessageChannel, or scheduler.postTask), letting the loop render, handle input, and fire timers between chunks. I'd size chunks by a time budget (~5ms) rather than a fixed count, and surface progress via a callback. For idle-time work I'd use requestIdleCallback, and for animation-synced work requestAnimationFrame.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cooperative time-slicing scheduler built on event-loop yielding.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Synchronous processing of large datasets blocks the single thread, freezing paint and input; yielding keeps the page responsive.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each tick processes work until a time budget is hit, then returns control by queuing the next chunk as a macrotask, so the loop can render and handle events before the next slice.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It's the core idea behind React's concurrent rendering and any responsive heavy-compute UI; it tests deep event-loop and performance understanding.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: React's scheduler slices rendering across tasks using a MessageChannel so high-priority input isn't blocked by low-priority rendering.

nestedTopics.title: Time-slicing
nestedTopics.explanation: Process within a small time budget per tick, then yield.

nestedTopics.title: Yield primitives
nestedTopics.explanation: setTimeout, MessageChannel, scheduler.postTask, requestIdleCallback each yield with different priority/timing.

nestedTopics.title: Backpressure & progress
nestedTopics.explanation: Report progress and allow cancellation between chunks.

followUps.question: Why not use microtasks to yield between chunks?
followUps.answer: Microtasks don't yield to rendering or input — they'd starve the loop. Macrotasks (or requestAnimationFrame) give the browser a chance to paint between chunks.

followUps.question: When would a Web Worker be better?
followUps.answer: For sustained heavy CPU work, offloading to a worker keeps the main thread fully free; the scheduler approach suits work that must touch the DOM or stay on the main thread.

productionDeepDive.architecture: The event loop is the substrate every async architecture sits on: data fetching, state updates, animation, and scheduling all coordinate through its queues. Frameworks build their own schedulers (React's scheduler, Vue's nextTick) on top of microtasks and macrotasks to batch and prioritize work.
productionDeepDive.performance: Responsiveness depends on keeping individual tasks short (under ~50ms) so the loop can render and handle input between them. Long synchronous tasks and microtask floods are the two main causes of jank; chunking and yielding fix them.
productionDeepDive.security: The event loop itself isn't a security boundary, but timing-sensitive code (e.g., relying on callback ordering) can introduce race conditions; treat ordering as defined by the spec, not by luck.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As app complexity grows, scheduling matters more: prioritize user-blocking work, defer idle work with requestIdleCallback, and offload sustained CPU work to Web Workers to keep the main loop free.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Code that relies on subtle micro/macro ordering is fragile; prefer explicit async/await and clear scheduling primitives over clever queue tricks so behavior is obvious to the next reader.
productionDeepDive.observability: Chrome DevTools' Performance panel shows the main-thread task timeline; the Long Tasks API and PerformanceObserver flag tasks that block the loop, and INP/responsiveness metrics quantify the user impact.

caseStudies.problem: Large render trees blocked the main thread and froze input.
caseStudies.solution: A scheduler that time-slices rendering across macrotasks (via MessageChannel), yielding to the event loop between units.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More scheduling overhead and complexity for far better responsiveness.
caseStudies.lessons: Cooperative yielding to the event loop is how you keep heavy work from freezing the UI.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript is single-threaded; the event loop interleaves sync code, microtasks, and macrotasks so async work never blocks the thread.
When the call stack empties, the loop drains the ENTIRE microtask queue, then runs exactly one macrotask, then repeats.
Promise callbacks (microtasks) always run before setTimeout callbacks (macrotasks), regardless of scheduling order.
setTimeout(fn, 0) is deferred to a future tick — it runs only after sync code and all microtasks finish.
A microtask that keeps scheduling microtasks starves the loop, freezing timers and rendering; yield with macrotasks to stay responsive.
